Data source overview  
This short conference paper (Simonyan, Vedaldi & Zisserman, 2014) proposes two gradient-based techniques for visualising deep convolutional image-classification models: (1) iteratively optimising an input image to maximise a chosen class score and (2) computing a per-pixel class-saliency map for a given input.  The authors show that resulting saliency maps can be used for weakly-supervised object segmentation and relate both techniques to “deconvolutional networks”.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[87]  
The extracted knowledge fabric captures the full causal path from the high-level interpretability risk through theoretical foundations, design reasoning, concrete mechanisms, empirical evidence, and to two actionable interventions.  Confidence is reduced slightly because only the abstract was available, limiting detail for evidence strength and implementation maturity.

Inference strategy justification  
The source does not explicitly state “risk” or “AI safety”; moderate inference (edge confidence = 2) was applied to map the implicit safety-relevant risk (lack of interpretability) and to translate the visualisation techniques into concrete safety interventions (audits during fine-tuning and pre-deployment).

Extraction completeness explanation  
Every distinct claim supporting the reasoning path (risk→problem→insight→rationale→mechanism→evidence) is decomposed into a node (total 11 nodes ≈ 15 per 5 k words guideline).  All nodes inter-connect; no satellites remain.  Framework names (“gradient-based visualisation”) are decomposed into component mechanisms.

Key limitations  
• Only qualitative evidence is provided in the abstract, so validation edge confidence is medium.  
• Real-world deployment evidence is absent, so intervention maturity is set to 3 (prototype).  
• Section titles were not available; “Paper abstract” is used as the closest reference throughout.
